own_scenes.desc: Sintetizado mientras se desarrollaba la bomba atómica, el LSD fue con ella el disolvente más potente de la cultura de los sesenta: «la única respuesta a la bomba» (George Andrews). Convertía el existencialismo atómico en un presente eterno sin lenguaje fuera del pensamiento oriental, hacía ridículos la competencia y el materialismo y abría una brecha sin precedentes entre quienes lo tomaban y quienes no. Dylan lo probó en mayo de 1964; un dentista se lo puso en el café a Lennon y Harrison en marzo de 1965. Seguía siendo legal en el otoño de 1965 y ya no lo controlaba Sandoz sino los contrabandistas: Timothy Leary predicaba una revolución de valores y la «Psychedelic Experience», Ken Kesey y los Merry Pranksters hacían Acid Tests caóticos, John Esam distribuía desde el 101 de Cromwell Road y Michael Hollingshead abrió en Londres el World Psychedelic Centre. En los primeros meses de 1966 pasó al centro de la escena y llegó la reacción: redada en el WPC, reportajes del News of the World, del People y de Life (25 de marzo), condena de treinta años a Leary por marihuana (que pidió una moratoria en abril), Sandoz cortó el suministro, el Gavin Report vetó «Eight Miles High» y «Rainy Day Women», Donovan fue el primer pop star detenido (junio) y California y Nevada prohibieron su posesión. Las primeras batallas las ganaron las autoridades, pero el genio ya había salido de la botella.

influences.name: La bomba y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: LSD opened a window into another world, but it was so strong that it easily derailed the fragile and the unwary.
refs.para: LSD opened a window into another world, but it was so strong that it easily derailed the fragile and the unwary. This is the contradiction that ‘The Third Eye’ encodes. Lyrically and vocally, it captures a moment of visionary transcendence. The rational mind seeks to define the experience in positive, if awestruck terms. But if the words speak of premature maturity, the explosive, chaotic intensity of the performance tells you that the whole experience is all too much. The listener is left with a disturbed aftertaste, a growl of chemical electricity that is anything but resolved or peaceful.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: Along with the bomb, it was the single most powerful dissolving agent in sixties culture.
refs.para: ‘Soldiers, take orders only from the rainbow alliance! Peace to the world,’ the poet George Andrews wrote in early 1966. ‘LSD is the only answer to the atom bomb.’ Acid took the existentialism that seemed like the only viable response to a world where instant atomisation was possible, if not likely, and transformed it into an eternal present for which there was barely a language yet outside the furthest reaches of Eastern thought. Along with the bomb, it was the single most powerful dissolving agent in sixties culture. After its arrival, nothing would ever be the same.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: No drug before or since has driven such a wedge between those who partook and those who did not.
refs.para: By the beginning of 1966, there were psychedelic districts in several major cities – London, Los Angeles and San Francisco, in particular – all of which had their own venues, their own groups and their own subcultures based around clothes, print, music and drugs. The traditional youthful artistic desire to create one’s own world was heightened by LSD. No drug before or since has driven such a wedge between those who partook and those who did not.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: On 25 March, a few days after the British exposés, Life magazine came out with its LSD cover story.
refs.para: On 25 March, a few days after the British exposés, Life magazine came out with its LSD cover story. Based around photos taken by Lawrence Schiller at the 25 February Acid Test in Hollywood, the anonymous text amplified the horrors: ‘The colorless, odorless, tasteless substance called LSD can be made in any college chemistry lab. A black market dose costs only $3 to $5. But that is enough to send a person on a 10-hour “trip” – sometimes into a world of beatific serenity and shimmering insight, sometimes to frenzy and terror.’
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: The first skirmishes in the LSD battle had been won, decisively, by the authorities. But it was too late: the genie was out of the bottle.
refs.para: The first skirmishes in the LSD battle had been won, decisively, by the authorities. But it was too late: the genie was out of the bottle. LSD was an extremely powerful dissolving agent, with a great ability to shape-shift and mutate, and its ability to transcend social and legal structures had already been observed. The siren call of self-discovery and instant transcendence – as broadcast by the sequence of extraordinary records in early 1966 – would not be silenced. The messages had been well heard.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

own_scenes.family: Funk psicodélico y black rock: Sly, Hendrix
own_scenes.desc: La revolución negra sacudió también a la juventud blanca: la cuestión moral de los derechos civiles, el racismo familiar, la atracción por la cultura negra, el miedo al reclutamiento y las drogas. Dylan y los Beatles convirtieron el rock en forma de vida. Sgt. Pepper (1967), de unos Beatles criados con Chuck Berry («a mí no me ha pasado nada desde 1958, cuando oí el rock and roll negro», dijo Lennon), abrió la era psicodélica que influiría en Electric Ladyland de Hendrix y en el Free Your Mind… de Funkadelic; Sly salió en el Ed Sullivan con uniforme de banda, y de ahí viene el púrpura de Prince. La contracultura sintetizó jazz, R&B, pop, rock y folk en formas largas, espectáculos de luces y tecnología, rasgos que el black rock (Hendrix, Sly, Funkadelic, War, Ohio Players, los Isley, Bar-Kays) llevó al funk. En Woodstock (1969) brillaron Hendrix, Sly y Santana. Las muertes de Hendrix, Joplin y Morrison, Altamont, Kent State y Jackson State acabaron con la idea de que el rock cambiaría el mundo; en la música negra el funk mantuvo vivos esos ideales.

influences.name: De los derechos civiles al Black Power

refs.q: The transformation of the black community in the 1960s generated a similar upheaval in white America.
refs.para: The transformation of the black community in the 1960s generated a similar upheaval in white America. This change was felt among white youth for many reasons, among which were the moral quagmire of civil rights, their own uptight and racist family backgrounds, their personal attractions to black culture, the life-threatening fear of the Vietnam War draft, and the influence of mind-altering drugs.

refs.q: But the ideals still remained—and in black music, it would be The Funk that would keep those ideals fresh
refs.para: The 1970 and 1971 deaths of Hendrix, Janis Joplin, and Jim Morrison; the murder in full view at the Rolling Stones Altamont rock concert; the police killings at student protests at Jackson State and Kent State; and the sound defeat of Democratic presidential hopeful George McGovern in 1972 put an end to the idea that rock and roll could change the world. But the ideals still remained—and in black music, it would be The Funk that would keep those ideals fresh, and keep the possibilities infinite.

own_scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 la palabra «psychedelic» llegó a Gran Bretaña: el Melody Maker la presentó el 22 de octubre como «el gran contraataque americano» y la prensa la aplicó a los Move, Creation, los Who y los californianos Misunderstood («vamos de viaje al subconsciente»): freak-outs, volumen y asalto sonoro. Fue el momento en que empezó el rock: virtuosismo, improvisación y ambición, aún contenidos en el single. Cream, tres veteranos del R&B, sacó «I Feel Free»; Jimi Hendrix, llegado en septiembre con Chas Chandler, era el negro americano empapado de soul, blues, Dylan y ácido que los británicos imitaban: «Hey Joe» y «Stone Free» («Free Feeling»). Donovan volvió con «Sunshine Superman». El 23 de diciembre abrió UFO en el Blarney Club, la primera noche del underground, con Pink Floyd en improvisaciones de diez minutos; en Nochevieja, Psychedelicamania en el Roundhouse con los Move, Pink Floyd y los Who. Los mods quedaban atrás.

influences.name: La India en el pop: sitar y raga rock

refs.q: The word had filtered into the UK in autumn 1966.
refs.para: The word had filtered into the UK in autumn 1966. On 22 October, the Melody Maker offered a guide to ‘psychedelic – the new in-word’. What it really added up to was ‘the great American comeback’: ‘A wave of powerful new groups, heavily armed with hits, are saturation bombing the American chart front, and threaten to start shooting down British groups on home ground … the Association, Monkees, Left Banke, Happenings, Young Rascals, Thirteenth Floor Elevators, McCoys, Positively Thirteen O’Clock, the Fugs, Love …
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: It wasn’t called that yet in the UK, but late 1966 was the moment when rock began.
refs.para: It wasn’t called that yet in the UK, but late 1966 was the moment when rock began. There was need for a new word to describe pop, which was no longer just an industrial process but the principal expressive form of the new massed youth society, and as such freighted with demands and ideas that would prove impossible to contain within the confines of a Top 40 chart or even a single. It was no longer pure commerce and simple good times, but the sound of a new freedom and a generational confidence.
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: Freedom was also at issue on both sides of the first Jimi Hendrix Experience single, released that month.
refs.para: Freedom was also at issue on both sides of the first Jimi Hendrix Experience single, released that month. ‘Hey Joe’ took the 1966 teen band staple, slowed it down, and then wrenched it inside out. To Tony Hall, who previewed it in Record Mirror, it had ‘quite the funkiest rhythm feel I’ve ever heard in this country. Quite Atlanticish.’ That same week, Hendrix gave an interview to the paper. ‘We don’t want to be classed in any category,’ he told Peter Jones. ‘If it must have a tag, I’d like it to be called “Free Feeling”. It’s a mixture of rock, freak-out, blues and rave music.’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: The brainchild of Joe Boyd and John Hopkins, the club night was an immediate success.
refs.para: The brainchild of Joe Boyd and John Hopkins, the club night was an immediate success. Around 400 people turned up and the Pink Floyd improvised at length. Peter Jenner remembered that ‘what had been the guitar break was becoming long waffly solos, so it seemed like the average song was about ten minutes long’. These extended, often textural explorations were an ideal soundtrack for the club. ‘You’d drop acid and arrive blotto,’ author Jenny Fabian recalled. ‘It was like descending into a subterranean world of dreams.’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

similar_scenes.name: Los primeros discos de ácido
similar_scenes.author: Jon Savage
similar_scenes.desc: «The Third Eye» de los Dovers (abril de 1966) es uno de los primeros intentos de reproducir el viaje de LSD en un disco y de los más exactos: fanfarria oriental, drones a lo Ravi Shankar, doce cuerdas de raga, melodía horizontal sin cambios de acorde, voz de «místico punk» y una espiral casi fuera de control. Dura 135 segundos pero condensa una experiencia de ocho horas. Grupo de instituto de Santa Bárbara que había hecho folk rock en Gold Star, se rehízo a comienzos de 1966 animado a «viajar por el bien de la banda»; el guitarrista Bruce Clawson tradujo su asombro y su terror en un formato pop. El título viene del best seller de Lobsang Rampa (en realidad Cyril Hoskin, de Devon), que también usaron Dylan y los 13th Floor Elevators de Austin, formados expresamente para difundir la conciencia LSD. Aquellos primeros discos de ácido no eran beatíficos sino crudos, salvajes y amenazantes: «The Trip» de Kim Fowley, «Ain’t It Hard» de los Gypsy Trips, «Free Advice» de The Great!! Society!!. Sin una gran discográfica detrás, «The Third Eye» cayó en el vacío, y Clawson oyó «Eight Miles High» en la radio unas semanas después.

similar_scenes.name: San Francisco: Acid Tests y Haight-Ashbury
similar_scenes.author: Jon Savage
similar_scenes.desc: A principios de 1966 había distritos psicodélicos con locales, grupos, ropa, impresos y drogas propios en Londres, Los Ángeles y San Francisco. Los Merry Pranksters de Ken Kesey convirtieron su desafío «Can You Pass the Acid Test?» en fiestas de luces, cine y sonido grabado y devuelto al instante: la segunda, en San José en diciembre de 1965 tras un concierto de los Stones, y nueve más en los tres primeros meses de 1966 (cinco en Los Ángeles, una en Watts). Los beats se habían mudado de North Beach a Haight-Ashbury; los Thelin abrieron la Psychedelic Shop y con Stewart Brand se hizo el Trips Festival (6.000 personas). La banda sonora era Rubber Soul. El caos sustituía al cuidado de Leary por el «set and setting»: en el Acid Test de Watts, Ken Babbs amplificó por micrófono los gritos de una chica en pleno mal viaje.

similar_scenes.name: El soul se vuelve funky
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: Tras la Bomba de James Brown, el soul dio un giro radical: el acento en el primer tiempo se oyó en «Superstition» de Stevie Wonder, «Inner City Blues» de Marvin Gaye y «Cloud Nine» de los Temptations; lo que empezó como un efecto se volvió norma, y el jam funk pasó a ser imprescindible para que un artista negro llegara a la gente en los setenta. Marvin Gaye preguntó «What’s Goin’ On».

similar_scenes.name: Motown, Norman Whitfield y la psicodelia soul
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: El imperio de Berry Gordy fue un fenómeno de capitalismo negro, pero en los setenta solo sobrevivieron los artistas que escribían su material (Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, Smokey Robinson, Michael Jackson). Norman Whitfield, que pasó de chupatintas a productor, le dio un filo más áspero («I Heard It Through the Grapevine» de Gladys Knight) y, mientras Sly arrasaba en 1968, cambió el sonido de los Temptations: temas largos con guitarras rockeras, efectos espaciales, drogas («Cloud Nine», «Psychedelic Shack», «Ball of Confusion») y orgullo negro, ropa a lo Hendrix y, al final, «Papa Was a Rollin’ Stone» (1972), soul con mensaje. La huella de P-Funk era clara (Eddie Hazel y Billy Nelson tocan en «Shakey Ground»); Whitfield convirtió a los Undisputed Truth en una banda de black rock pintada de plata. Los músicos de sesión, los Funk Brothers, trabajaban en la sombra: el bajista James Jamerson, que sacaba líneas de cómo hablaba o caminaba la gente, influyó a todos. Cuando Motown se mudó a Los Ángeles, la banda se quedó en Detroit y la magia se perdió.

podcast.title: Element of German Rock
podcast.body: Psychedelic music was a key element incorporated into the emerging distinctly German rock sound by the end of the 1960s, which also featured improvisation and structured compositions that diverged from blues traditions or normal rock conventions. "It had elements of psychedelic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hapshash and the Colored Coat's "Heavy Metal" Album
podcast.body: The 1967 album "The Human Host and the Heavy Metal Kids" by Hapshash and the Colored Coat, despite its title, is described as having a psychedelic musical style rather than resembling what would later be known as heavy metal. "But if we listen to the record, it's more psychedelic than aliens."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rickenbacker Sound Preference (1960s)
podcast.body: The characteristic "jangle" or "chime" sound of Rickenbacker guitars appealed to artists experimenting with the new psychedelic sounds of the 1960s. "the unique sound of the Rickenbacher made it a favorite among... those into the new psychedelic sounds of the 1960s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2
